title: Put a medicine cabinet's sliding mirror door back on its bottom track and slide it shut
instruction: The front mirror door of this medicine cabinet has come off its bottom track. Put it back on its track and slide it shut.
context: Surface-mount bypass medicine cabinets, with two 1/8 in mirror doors in an integral top and bottom track, are a common fitting in rental and older bathrooms. The doors go in by lifting them into the deep upper channel and dropping them into the shallow lower one, and that same clearance lets a door's foot jump its bottom channel. The door then hangs from the top channel and leans out over the basin. If you slide it like that, the foot drags further out until about 1.1 kg of glass falls into the sink. Pushing the foot in without lifting the door jams it against the channel's lip.
real_product: Ketcham Medicine Cabinets, Sliding Door series, surface mounted (SDL-2419 lit version verified; the plain SD-2419 is assumed to be the same family). Overall size 24 x 19-1/2 x 7-1/2 in, body 4-1/2 in deep. 2 sliding doors of 1/8 in polished-edge electrosilver mirror. "Integral Track System". Acrylic slider handles stuck on with vinyl glazing tape. Sources: Ketcham's technical data sheet and product page (ketchamcabinets.com/all-products/sdl-2419, data sheet linked there), and the "Sliding Door Series - Surface Mounted" install sheet (st.hzcdn.com/hfiles/66b48ff0006c915f_7839). The install sheet says to allow 1 in above obstructions and that the doors exceed the body by 1 in. Mechanism source: the Grainger sliding-door cabinet sheet 446L98 says "Install sliding doors in cabinet by lifting into upper channel and dropping them down into lower channel. NOTE: Insert right hand door in the rear channel first." I saw this only as a search snippet, because the PDF host would not resolve from here. Channel depths are not published by Ketcham. A comparable CRL D718 upper plastic track for 1/8 in panels is 1/2 in tall with a 0.198 in opening (dkhardware listing); the lower channel depth (assumed about 3/16 in) is not verified. Correction to the idea: a 24 x 19.5 in cabinet has doors of about 31 x 45 cm, 3.2 mm glass, about 1.1 kg each. The idea's 30 x 60 cm, 4 mm, 1.3 kg is wrong (those dimensions would weigh 1.8 kg). The real product keeps both the fault and the lift-in, drop-in skill,
fault: The front door's foot is outside the front bottom channel, in front of the channel's outer lip. The door hangs from the top channel tilted about 5 degrees outward, with its bottom edge about 4 cm proud of the cabinet face. The rear door is seated in the rear channels at the other end. Caveat: when a door jumps the track in real life, the foot more often rides on top of the outer lip. From there the fix is only a nudge back, with no lift needed, which makes the task trivial. The hanging-out state above is plausible, but in simulation it is a friction wedge that is sensitive to tuning.
skill: Get under the door's 3.2 mm bottom edge with both grippers spread about 20 cm apart, so the door doesn't rack in its channels. Lift it 5 to 8 mm, which sends the top deeper into the top channel. Swing the foot back over the front channel (not the rear one, and without disturbing the rear door) and lower it in. Then slide it to its closed end by pushing low on the door or its handle. Taking the door fully out and refitting it is also a valid route, but it needs the same lift into the top channel and drop into the bottom one.

grep -iE over pipeline/known_tasks.tsv (2,479 rows, refreshed 17 Nov) for: mirror, medicine, bypass, sliding, slide.*door, track, channel, derail, popped, jumped, window, sash, screen, insect, storm, shower, cabinet door, glass, pane, panel, wardrobe, closet, refit, reseat, rehang, lift-off, hinge. I read the reviews of the nearest PRs.

The killer is #1911 "Put an insect screen back in its window, seated on all four sides: top up against its plungers, swing in, let down". It is PENDING: revision TK-M74T74 is waiting for review. It belongs to another team (whose posts are from lianegalanti). Its first review asked only for seating on all four sides, so importance was not challenged. The screen has a deep head channel, a shallow sill channel with a lip, and the method is to push the top up into the head, swing the bottom in over the lip, and let it down. That is exactly this idea's forced skill. The idea's note "none does the lift-in/drop-in re-entry" is wrong; the grep missed #1911 because its title is "Add refit-window-insect-screen task". While #1911 is held this would be a near-duplicate, and if #1911 is accepted it becomes "different object, same skill". The mirror door's fix is also a subset of the screen task: the door starts already hanging in the top channel, and it needs no plungers or side tracks.

- #473 (block jammed in a sliding-door track): final rejection for miniaturization, and because lifting the door out earned full credit.
- #1796 (key in a display-case track): final rejection as a variant, and as not core work.
- #2083 (miniature panel in slots): final rejection for miniaturization.
- #751 (stiff sliding window): revising; a different skill (pulling against resistance).
- #2160 (swollen sliding window): final rejection as a duplicate
reach_check:
I used yam_arena.ik.solve, sourced from yam.env, on the LEFT arm (the right is mirror-symmetric, and the first pass showed identical numbers). Each pose was tried with 11 to 17 random seeds plus READY, and roll about the approach axis was swept in 22.5-degree steps. Pass means under 1.5 mm and under 2 degrees.

Real-height layout: arm bases on the counter at z 0.75, wall x 0.55, cabinet bottom 18 in above the counter (z 1.198), front door plane x 0.439, door bottom z 1.212, door top z 1.67.
- Fingers under the door's bottom edge, approach +x horizontal or pitched up 20 degrees (0.45 m above the base): OK for every y from -0.10 to +0.40.
- Handle zone, 10 cm above the bottom edge, approach +x: OK for y +0.10 to +0.40; misses by 17 to 50 mm at y 0 to -0.10.
- Pinching the glass 4 cm above its bottom with a sideways approach: OK only at y +0.10.
- Door face at mid-height (0.69 m above the base): misses by 55 to 146 mm at every y.
- 4 cm below the door top: misses by 190 to 280 mm.

Low mount (15 in above the counter): mid-height still misses by 12 to 93 mm, and the top by 146 mm or more. With an 18 in vanity (wall x 0.47), the under-edge and handle-zone poses pass at every y and the top still misses by over 150 mm.

Conclusion: at real height the robot can work only the lower ~12 cm of the door. That is enough for the lift, swing-in, drop and slide-shut by the bottom edge and handle, because the top is captured in its channel. The cabinet stays at its real height with nothing mo
reviewer_reasons:
wide-funnel deepen, 17 Nov: killed. Kill reason: the core skill is the same lift-in, swing-in, drop-in re-entry as pending #1911 (insect screen in head and sill channels), which another team holds. It would be judged a near-duplicate now, and "different object, same skill" if #1911 is accepted. The mirror version is also a strict subset of it: no plungers, no side tracks, and the door starts half-fitted.

Further risks:
- The lift is only 5 to 8 mm, so the difficulty may be judged too small, in line with #2127.
- The most common real jumped-track state, with the foot riding on the outer lip, needs only a nudge back. The hanging-out-over-the-lip fault is a friction wedge in simulation that is sensitive to tuning, which risks reading as a staged fault.
- Channel depths are not published for Ketcham or Zenna. The mechanism source is a search snippet of a Grainger sheet that I could not download.
- No SimReady medicine cabinet, vanity or sink exists, so the main object is all primitives: an "egregious simplification" risk.
- 3.2 mm glass in 5 mm channels, with gripper contact on a 3.2 mm edge, is fragile in PhysX.
- The robot can reach only the lower ~12 cm of the door at real height. That is fine for this skill, but a reviewer may ask how a person steadies the top.
- The safety framing (glass into the basin) would likely be read as object protection, so it stays in Societal relatability, which is broad but is how bypass cabinets are used in many homes.
